content: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of skin snips and skin snip microscopy (or non-exposure methods) were evaluated in diagnostic studies to assess their effectiveness in detecting Onchocerca volvulus. The Ov-16 serology test, which detects antibodies against a 16-amino acid signal peptide of Onchocerca volvulus, was compared to skin snip microscopy in various studies conducted in endemic regions such as Ghana, Cameroon, Sierra Leone, and other African countries. These studies also included data from the Americas, such as Ecuador, Guatemala, and Mexico. The Ov-16 serology test was often used as an index test, while skin snip microscopy served as the reference standard. In one study conducted in Mexico, 13,400 black flies were tested using the O-150 PCR method, which employed high-throughput automated DNA isolation with silica-coated paramagnetic beads. This was compared to phenol-chloroform DNA extraction methods. Another study in Ghana and Burkina Faso tested 25,548 black flies using the O-150 PCR pool screen method, with fly dissection as the reference test. These studies demonstrated the utility of PCR-based methods in detecting Onchocerca volvulus DNA in black flies, particularly in regions with ongoing transmission. The quality of evidence for skin snip microscopy and Ov-16 serology was rated as low due to indirectness, risk of bias, and imprecision. However, the quality of evidence for O-150 PCR (pool screen) in black flies was rated as high, as it was based on observational studies from multiple countries, providing better applicability and fewer concerns regarding indirectness. The main limitations of these studies included the lack of comparison groups, inconsistencies in the number of villages and individuals tested, and variability in the timing of mass drug administration (MDA) cessation. Observational studies in Guatemala examined 365 individuals ophthalmologically and 3,118 children serologically, collecting data during the post-treatment surveillance phase. These studies confirmed the interruption of transmission and elimination of onchocerciasis after MDA cessation. Skin snip microscopy and O-150 PCR reliably demonstrated the interruption of transmission after 12–16 years of MDA and elimination of onchocerciasis 2–5 years after MDA cessation. However, the reliability of skin snip microscopy as a gold-standard reference test was questioned, particularly in low-prevalence settings, as PCR-based methods likely have more accurate diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) characteristics. The sensitivity of O-150 PCR of skin snips compared to skin snip microscopy varied between 71% and 100%, while the sensitivity of Ov-16 serology compared to skin snip microscopy ranged from 81% to 98%. Specificity values for Ov-16 serology ranged from 89% to 98%. The overall quality of evidence for these comparisons was low, partly due to the case-control design of several studies and the lack of inclusion of individuals without onchocerciasis in some cases. Additionally, the applicability of results from studies conducted in the Americas to other regions, such as Africa, was limited. In Uganda, studies using Ov-16 serology in children and skin snip microscopy demonstrated the interruption of transmission in various foci, with some regions achieving elimination due to vector elimination. Similar findings were reported in Guatemala, Mexico, and Venezuela, where Ov-16 serology, O-150 PCR, and skin snip microscopy were used to confirm the interruption of transmission and elimination of onchocerciasis. However, in regions such as Cameroon and Nigeria, ongoing transmission was detected using these diagnostic methods. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported the certification of onchocerciasis elimination in several countries. However, no comparative studies of diagnostic tests or follow-up data from certification onwards were identified to assess the reliability of testing regimes. The lack of comparative data and the variability in testing methods and prevalence across regions highlight the need for standardized diagnostic approaches to confirm the interruption of transmission and elimination of onchocerciasis globally.
